Abstract 36

Polygenic scores (PGS) are typically derived from single-trait genome-wide association studies 37

(GWAS), yet many complex diseases arise from shared genetic liability distributed across 38

correlated clinical dimensions. Accordingly, disease risk depends not only on how genetic liability 39

is represented but also on the social context in which that liability is expressed. Whether 40

Here we constructed PGS for 35 orthogonal latent phenomic factors derived from 2,772 44

phenotypes in 361,114 UK Biobank (UKB) participants and evaluated their phenomic specificity, 45

cross-dataset portability and predictive performance relative to conventional disease-specific 46

PGS across the UKB holdout, Mass General Brigham Biobank and the All of Us (AoU) Research 47

Program. Factor-based PGS showed widespread, biologically coherent phenome-wide 48

associations that were reproducible across biobanks and ancestries. Their predictive utility, 49

however, was strongly disease dependent. For asthma, a respiratory factor PGS outperformed 50

an internally derived disease-specific PGS and showed superior cross-ancestry portability, 51

retaining 41.5% of European-ancestry predictive accuracy in African-ancestry individuals, 52

compared with 22.9% for an asthma PGS derived from the largest available multi-ancestry 53

GWAS. By contrast, disease-specific PGS remained superior for coronary artery disease (CAD) 54

and type 2 diabetes (T2D). These findings suggest that phenome-derived aggregation is most 55

beneficial when disease-specific GWAS incompletely capture underlying liability, including 56

settings of biological heterogeneity or imprecise phenotyping. 57

58

We then evaluated SDoH in AoU as a complementary axis shaping prevalent disease prediction 59

beyond genetic susceptibility. Across all three diseases, SDoH contributed substantial and largely 60

independent predictive information beyond the disease-optimal genetic model. SDoH also 61

modified how genetic liability translated into observed disease prevalence: for asthma and CAD, 62

genetic stratification attenuated with increasing social burden, whereas this attenuation was 63

substantially weaker for T2D. As a result, the same genetic percentile corresponded to different 64

standardized predicted prevalences across social strata, reflecting disease-specific shifts in 65

baseline prevalence, genetic gradients and calibration. 66

67

Together, these findings indicate that disease risk is shaped by both genetic liability and the social 68

context in which that liability is realized. Phenome-derived PGS improve prediction under specific 69

architectural conditions, whereas social context independently modifies the performance, 70

calibration and interpretation of genetic risk across populations. 71

Introduction 72

Polygenic scores (PGS) quantify inherited susceptibility to complex traits and diseases by 73

aggregating genetic effects identified through genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Most 74

PGS are derived from GWAS of a single observed phenotype, such as disease diagnoses or 75

quantitative measurements. While effective for targeted outcomes, single-phenotype PGS may 76

incompletely capture the underlying liability of complex diseases, especially when disease 77

definitions are heterogeneous, noisy or sensitive to ascertainment. This limitation is particularly 78

pronounced for complex diseases that lie along continuous spectra rather than discrete binary 79

states. Data-driven representations that integrate information across correlated measurements 80

may therefore provide more stable targets for genetic prediction1,2. 81

Modern population biobanks enable unprecedented phenotyping scales, collecting thousands of 83

correlated clinical, behavioral, and socio-environmental measures for each participant. This 84

phenotypic richness reveals structured covariance across traits, reflecting shared biological 85

pathways, common disease processes and socially patterned exposures. Modeling each 86

phenotype independently for PGS construction therefore overlooks this structure and treats 87

correlated manifestations of disease as separate outcomes. Several approaches have sought to 88

incorporate information from multiple traits for genetic prediction. Some combine phenotype- 89

specific PGS downstream using linear or penalized regression models3,4. Others, including multi- 90

trait GWAS methods such as MTAG5, jointly analyze genetically correlated traits to improve 91

association estimates for selected outcomes. Although these approaches can improve prediction, 92

they remain anchored to predefined observed phenotypes or prespecified target outcomes. They 93

combine information across traits without redefining the unit of genetic signal itself. 94

95

Phenome-wide factor analysis provides an alternative framework by distilling thousands of 96

heterogeneous phenotypes into a small number of latent dimensions that capture stable and 97

genetically coherent axes of phenomic variation6. GWAS of factor scores thus shifts the unit of 98

genetic association from individual phenotypes to latent phenomic dimensions. Because factor 99

structures are cohort-specific and not directly transferable across datasets, however, it remains 100

unknown whether genetic liabilities derived from such factors can generalize across populations 101

and improve prediction of clinically relevant diseases relative to conventional disease-specific 102

PGS. 103

104

A second limitation of polygenic prediction is that its performance depends not only on how 105

genetic liability is represented, but also on the context in which that liability is expressed. PGS 106

performance varies across contexts, such as age, socioeconomic status and other environmental 107

settings7–9. Yet, these contextual differences are typically described post hoc rather than modeled 108

explicitly. Social determinants of health (SDoH)10 provide structured and measurable 109

representations of such context, capturing dimensions of social and environmental risk that 110

influence disease burden and may modify the expression, interpretation and calibration of 111

inherited susceptibility. Despite extensive epidemiological evidence linking social exposures to 112

health outcomes, most polygenic prediction frameworks incorporate few explicit SDoH measures, 113

limiting their ability to characterize how genetic risk manifests across heterogeneous 114

environments9,11,12. 115

116

Here, we evaluate phenome-derived factor-based PGS as genetic representations of latent 117

phenomic liability and assess their predictive utility across diseases and populations. Using factor 118

scores derived from 361,114 deeply phenotyped UK Biobank (UKB) participants, we construct 119

PGS for 35 orthogonal latent factors and benchmark their phenome-wide specificity, cross-cohort 120

generalizability and predictive performance against disease-specific PGS. We then integrate 121

structured SDoH indices in the All of Us Research Program (AoU), where rich survey-derived 122

social measures enable explicit evaluation of social context beyond the disease-optimal genetic 123

model, and test whether social context reshapes the performance, calibration and interpretation 124

of genetic risk. Through this integrated framework, we define when phenome-derived genetic 125

Results 128

Previous phenome-wide factor analysis in 361,114 unrelated European (EUR) individuals in UKB 129

identified 35 latent factors distilled from 2,772 heterogeneous phenotypes6. These factors 130

spanned 6 broad domains: clinical disease and health history, lifestyle and behavior, mental 131

health and cognition, physical measurements, socio-environmental context and biomarkers 132

(Table S1). Using GWAS of factor scores, we constructed PGS for each factor with PRS-CS13, 133

yielding genetic predictors of latent phenomic liability. Because latent factor scores are cohort- 134

specific and cannot be reconstructed outside the discovery cohort, we assessed factor-based 135

PGS through phenome-wide association analyses and predictive benchmarking across multiple 136

biobanks and ancestry groups. As a complementary component of the study, we evaluated SDoH 137

in AoU using structured indices derived from 29 variables spanning the five Healthy People 2030 138

domains10. We constructed both domain-specific scores and a composite SDoH index, then 139

examined their independent and joint contributions beyond the disease-optimal PGS, as well as 140

whether SDoH burden modified the performance, calibration, and interpretation of genetic risk 141

through interaction and stratified analyses. The overall analytical framework is summarized in Fig. 142

Factor-based PGS capture specific and reproducible phenomic structure 165

across biobanks and ancestries 166

To assess the phenomic specificity and generalizability of factor-based PGS, we conducted PGS- 167

pheWAS association analyses within each biobank-by-ancestry stratum, applying Bonferroni 168

correction based on the number of tested outcomes per stratum (Methods). Across biobanks, we 169

observed widespread and reproducible phenomic associations of factor-based PGS. Specifically, 170

we identified a total of 96, 698, and 3,869 significant PGS-PheCode associations out of 42,245, 171

115,253, and 190,785 tests in the UKB holdout, Mass General Brigham Biobank (MGBB), and 172

AoU, respectively (Table S2). Because factor models are invariant to sign, factor-PGS were 173

interpreted relative to dominant loadings defining each factor, such that positive and negative 174

associations denote concordant and discordant relationships with the corresponding latent 175

phenomic dimension. Under this convention, the majority of significant associations were positive 176

(84.9%), with a median OR of 1.12, while negative associations showed a median OR of 0.91. 177

The predominance of modest, directionally coherent effects across biobanks is consistent with 178

highly polygenic liability rather than cohort-specific artifacts. Both positive and negative 179

associations were biologically interpretable in the context of the constituent phenotypes defining 180

each factor. 181

182

The distribution of associations across factors revealed clear and structured phenomic structure 183

(Extended Data Figs. 1-2). Factors reflecting clinical disease and health history showed the 184

highest number of associations (2,199), followed by socio-environmental contexts (964) and 185

physical measurements (858). These patterns were consistent across biobanks despite 186

substantial differences in recruitment strategies, healthcare systems, and phenotype 187

ascertainment, indicating that factor-based PGS capture robust dimensions of genetic liability. 188

189

Factor-based PGS further exhibited strong phenotypic specificity consistent with the domains 190

captured by their constituent phenotypes. For example, the PGS derived from a respiratory 191

disease factor showed strong and selective associations with PheCodes within the respiratory 192

disease category across biobanks and ancestries. Asthma emerged as the top association in 193

each dataset, with ORs ranging from 1.32 in AoU and MGBB to 1.57 in the UKB holdout among 194

EUR individuals (Fig. 2). Consistent with domain specificity, the respiratory factor PGS showed 195

minimal enrichment for associations outside respiratory-related PheCode chapters (Table S2), 196

indicating that phenome-wide signal was concentrated within clinically coherent domains rather 197

than reflecting diffuse pleiotropy. In contrast, PGS derived from socio-demographic factors, such 198

as educational attainment, exhibited broader phenomic associations spanning multiple disease 199

categories, with ORs ranging from 0.84 to 1.70 (Fig. 2). These associations were not confined to 200

a single disease domain and included consistent enrichment for mental and behavioral disorders 201

across biobanks. This broader pattern likely reflects a combination of shared behavioral risk 202

profiles and socially patterned exposures, rather than a single underlying biological process. 203

To quantify phenomic structure at the level of disease categories, we performed enrichment 224

analyses assessing whether significant associations for each factor were disproportionately 225

concentrated within specific PheCode chapters. Within each biobank and ancestry, enrichment 226

Z-scores were computed using a hypergeometric framework that accounted for the number of 227

tested outcomes per factor and category (Methods; Supplementary Note 1). Meta-analysis of 228

enrichment statistics across biobanks revealed highly coherent and biologically interpretable 229

patterns (Fig. 3; Extended Data Fig. 3). Disease-oriented factors showed strong positive 230

enrichment for their corresponding clinical domains, particularly in EUR (median meta-analysis Z 231

= 15.22; range 3.80-21.22), with consistent but attenuated signals observed across other 232

ancestries. In contrast, socio-demographic and behavioral factors demonstrated broader but 233

generally weaker enrichment across multiple disease categories (median Z = 3.74; range 2.43- 234

17.86 in EUR), consistent with more diffuse cross-domain effects. 235

236

Importantly, these enrichment patterns were consistent across biobanks despite the non- 237

transferability of the underlying phenotypic factor structures (Table S3; Supplementary Figs. 1- 238

3). Although latent factors derived from deep phenotyping cannot be directly reconstructed in 239

external datasets, the associated liabilities manifested as stable and expected phenomic 240

signatures across independent populations–an importantly portable characteristic of phenome- 241

derived PGS. 242

243

Across ancestries, we observed strong concordance in the direction and relative magnitude of 244

associations. Among all significant associations, median ORs were 1.11 (s.d. = 0.13) across 411 245

associations in EUR, 1.19 (s.d. = 0.17) across 298 associations in Admixed American ancestry 246

(AMR), 1.15 (s.d. = 0.08) across 61 associations in individuals of African ancestry (AFR), 1.30 247

(s.d. = 0.13) across 38 associations in Central and South Asian ancestry (CSA), and 1.52 (s.d. = 248

0.17) across 9 associations in East Asian ancestry (EAS). An additional two associations were 249

observed in individuals of Middle Eastern ancestry. Among these, 411 associations were shared 250

by at least two ancestry groups, and effect sizes were strongly correlated across ancestry pairs 251

with adequate overlap (Pearson’s r = 0.80-0.89). Effect-size distributions were similarly 252

comparable across biobanks, with median ORs of 1.31 (s.d. = 0.21) in the UKB holdout, 1.11 (s.d. 253

= 0.13) in All of Us, and 1.12 (s.d. = 0.13) in MGBB, and 640 associations were replicated in at 254

least two biobanks. Overall, 50 associations involving 10 distinct factors and 28 PheCodes were 255

detected across all three biobanks in at least one ancestry group (Extended Data Fig. 4). 256

257

Together, these analyses indicate that factor-based PGS capture stable and interpretable 258

dimensions of genetic liability that manifest as reproducible phenomic signatures across 259

independent biobanks and populations. 260

Factor-based PGS outperform disease-specific scores for asthma 279

Asthma showed the strongest improvement in predictive performance for factor-based PGS. 280

Across EUR cohorts, the respiratory factor PGS performed comparably to or better than the 281

internally derived PheCode-based asthma PGS. The largest improvement was observed in UKB, 282

where factor PGS achieved 𝑅! = 0.045 (95% CI: 0.028-0.069) compared to 0.032 (0.018-0.052) 283

for asthma PGS, corresponding to a 41% relative gain (Fig. 4a; Table S5). This advantage 284

replicated in MGBB (+29%) and was near parity in the largest cohort, AoU (+3%). 285

286

The two PGS were moderately to strongly correlated across cohorts (Pearson’s 𝑟 = 0.67-0.70), 287

indicating substantial shared genetic liability. However, joint models including both scores 288

revealed that factor PGS captured independent predictive signals beyond asthma PGS (Fig. 4b; 289

Table S5). In UKB, factor PGS remained strongly associated with asthma (β = 0.363, p = 290

1.9×10⁻⁸), while asthma PGS became marginally non-significant (β = 0.124, p = 0.052). In MGBB, 291

both scores contributed independently, though the effect size of factor PGS was approximately 292

two-fold larger. In AoU, both scores contributed comparably, consistent with balanced predictive 293

signal in the largest cohort. 294

295

As a secondary benchmark, we compared the respiratory factor PGS with an asthma PGS derived 296

from the Global Biobank Meta-analysis Initiative (GBMI)14,15. Against this external benchmark, 297

factor PGS showed comparable performance in UKB (𝑅! = 0.045 vs 0.050), whereas GBMI PGS 298

exhibited increasing advantage in MGBB (50% higher) and AoU (77% higher), consistent with its 299

substantially larger discovery sample size (Extended Data Fig. 5). Despite this, factor PGS 300

showed markedly superior cross-ancestry portability, even though its underlying GWAS were 301

conducted solely in EUR participants, whereas the GBMI meta-analysis included multiple 302

ancestries. In AFR, factor PGS retained 41.5% of EUR predictive accuracy, compared to 22.9% 303

for GBMI PGS and 12.1% for the smaller internal PheCode-based PGS (Extended Data Fig. 6). 304

Similar advantages were observed in EAS and CSA, with comparable performance in AMR. 305

Disease-specific PGS outperform factor-based scores for cardiometabolic diseases 330

In contrast to asthma, disease-specific PGS consistently outperformed factor-based PGS for CAD 331

and T2D across cohorts. For CAD, disease-specific PGS showed higher predictive accuracy in 332

all three cohorts (Fig. 4). In UKB, CAD PGS achieved 𝑅! = 0.069 (0.048-0.091) compared with 333

0.043 (0.026-0.066) for the corresponding factor PGS (+60%). This advantage remained larger 334

in AoU (+73%) but was attenuated in the clinical cohort MGBB (+21%). The two scores were 335

highly correlated (𝑟 ≈ 0.68), reflecting substantial shared genetic architecture, yet joint modeling 336

indicated little additional contribution from factor-based PGS. Although factor and CAD GWAS 337

were highly genetically correlated (𝑟" = 0.88), pathway analysis revealed broader vascular and 338

structural pathway involvement for CAD GWAS, while the corresponding factor GWAS was more 339

narrowly enriched for lipoprotein and triglyceride-related processes (Supplementary Fig. 4). This 340

pattern is consistent with the factor’s dominant loadings on ischemic heart disease diagnoses 341

together with cardiovascular medications and high-cholesterol-related items. The same pattern 342

was observed in secondary comparisons with large public CAD GWAS-based PGS (Extended 343

Data Figs. 5 and 6). 344

345

A similar pattern was observed for T2D, with larger relative differences in predictive performance 346

between disease-specific and factor-based PGS. In UKB, PheCode-based T2D PGS achieved 347

𝑅! = 0.050 (0.032-0.074) compared to 0.032 (0.016-0.055) for factor PGS, representing a 56% 348

relative improvement; larger relative differences were observed in MGBB (+130%) and AoU 349

(+101%) (Fig. 4; Table S4). Although the two scores showed moderate correlation (𝑟 = 0.55- 350

0.56), joint modeling indicated that T2D PGS captured most predictive signals, with factor PGS 351

contributing minimal incremental value. These performance differences were concordant with 352

underlying genetic architecture. T2D GWAS exhibited modestly higher heritability (ℎ! = 0.052 ± 353

0.003 vs 0.043 ± 0.003; p = 0.03) and broader MAGMA enrichment (Supplementary Fig. 4), 354

whereas the corresponding factor was dominated by diabetes diagnosis together with 355

cholesterol-, medication-, and illness-burden-related items. Secondary benchmarking against 356

large public T2D GWAS likewise favored disease-specific PGS (Extended Data Figs. 5-6). 357

358

Discussion 584

This study shows that the utility of polygenic prediction depends on two related but distinct 585

features of disease risk: how genetic liability is represented and the context in which that liability 586

is expressed. Across multiple biobanks and ancestries, factor-based PGS captured phenomically 587

coherent and portable dimensions of genetic liability, but their predictive value was not universal. 588

Instead, the benefit of phenomic aggregation was disease dependent: it was most evident for 589

asthma, where a respiratory factor PGS better captured shared liability across heterogeneous 590

respiratory phenotypes than a matched disease-specific score, but limited for CAD and T2D, 591

where disease-specific GWAS provided a more complete representation of inherited risk. These 592

findings position phenome-derived PGS not as a general replacement for disease-specific scores, 593

but as a conditional alternative that is most useful when diagnosis-based GWAS incompletely 594

capture underlying liability, particularly in settings where disease definitions are heterogeneous, 595

noisy, or sensitive to ascertainment. 596

597

Our framework also differs from existing cross-trait approaches that seek to improve prediction 598

for a prespecified target outcome. Methods such as MTAG5 leverage cross-trait genetic 599

correlation at the GWAS stage to improve trait-specific association estimates, whereas multi-trait 600

PRS approaches, such as PRSmix+3 and GPSMult16,17, combine multiple trait-specific scores at 601

the prediction stage to optimize disease-specific performance. By contrast, we redefine the unit 602

of genetic signal itself by deriving PGS from unsupervised latent phenomic factors and then 603

testing whether these representations better capture disease liability than diagnosis-based 604

Asthma provides a clear example of such a setting. The respiratory factor PGS outperformed the 608

This advantage was accompanied by higher SNP-based heritability and broader pathway 611

enrichment, consistent with the possibility that factor-derived GWAS captured syndrome-level 612

incomplete genetic correlation with asthma across populations19,20. More broadly, these findings 616

suggest that phenotype definition, and not only discovery sample size, is an important determinant 617

of PGS portability. 618

619

An additional implication is that portability of factor-derived PGS does not require transferability 620

of the underlying phenotypic factor structure itself. Although latent factors derived from deep 621

phenotyping are cohort specific, the genetic liabilities they capture can still manifest as 622

reproducible phenomic signatures across independent datasets. This decoupling between factor 623

construction and external phenomic manifestation suggests that phenome-derived PGS may 624

provide a compact and biologically interpretable representation of liability even when the original 625

phenotypic architecture cannot be reconstructed outside the discovery cohort6. More generally, 626

differences across biobanks likely reflect not only genetic architecture and phenotype definition, 627

but also cohort-specific ascertainment and healthcare-system context21. 628

629

By contrast, CAD and T2D illustrate settings in which disease-specific GWAS remain more 630

informative than phenomic aggregation. In both diseases, the internally derived disease-specific 631

PGS outperformed the corresponding factor-based score, and larger public GWAS-based PGS 632

further outperformed both. In both cases, the corresponding factors appeared to capture clinically 633

broader mixtures of diagnosis, treatment, and comorbidity burden than the more specific inherited 634

liability represented by disease-specific GWAS. When disease-specific GWAS already provide a 635

strong and relatively complete model of inherited risk, broader phenomic representation offers 636

limited additional value. The concordance between predictive performance, genetic correlation, 637

SNP heritability and pathway enrichment supports this interpretation and helps define the 638

conditions under which phenome-derived PGS are most likely to improve disease risk prediction. 639

disease-oriented factors, which are plausibly anchored in shared pathophysiology, PGS derived 642

associations for socio-behavioral traits, including educational attainment and substance use, are 645

known to reflect a combination of direct genetic effects, gene-environment correlation and 646

environmental stratification24–26. Their broad associations, including enrichment for mental and 647

behavioral disorders across biobanks, may therefore reflect both meaningful predictive structure 648

A second major finding, observed in AoU, is that SDoH contributed substantial and largely 653

independent predictive information beyond the disease-optimal genetic model. Across asthma, 654

A particularly important implication is that social context altered not only the incremental predictive 664

value of PGS, but also its calibration. For asthma and CAD, increasing SDoH burden attenuated 665

the incremental AUC contributed by PGS and shifted the relationship between genetic percentile 666

and predicted prevalence. For T2D, this attenuation was weaker, indicating relative preservation 667

of genetic stratification despite increasing social burden. Across all three diseases, however, the 668

same genetic percentile did not correspond to the same predicted prevalence across social strata. 669

This is clinically important because it means that the interpretation of PGS is context dependent 670

even when the score itself is fixed. In this setting, SDoH is not merely an additive predictor, but a 671

determinant of how genetic risk should be interpreted, calibrated and translated into predicted 672

prevalence. More broadly, these findings show that structured social context can systematically 673

reshape the practical meaning of genetic risk, although the magnitude and form of this effect will 674

depend on the population and measurement context in which SDoH are assessed27. Accordingly, 675

these estimates should be interpreted as context-dependent rather than assumed to transfer 676

unchanged across healthcare systems or populations. 677

Importantly, these context-dependent patterns are scale dependent. For asthma and CAD, 679

genetic stratification as measured by incremental AUC and odds-ratio gradients attenuated with 680

increasing SDoH burden, whereas predicted-prevalence differences across genetic strata were 681

prevalence differences across SDoH strata. These findings are therefore consistent rather than 684

contradictory, and emphasize that clinically relevant effect modification may be more apparent on 685

additive or predicted-prevalence-difference scales than on multiplicative scales alone. 686

687

These results have two broader implications. First, they argue against one-size-fits-all approaches 688

to polygenic prediction, consistent with prior recommendations emphasizing trait-specific model 689

optimization20,28. The optimal genetic representation of disease risk differs across outcomes, and 690

broader aggregation across phenotypes is most useful when it captures coherent latent liability 691

that is only partially represented by diagnosis-based GWAS. Second, they show that improving 692

Methods 720

Study design 721

We evaluated disease prediction along two complementary axes: how genetic liability is 722

represented and the social context in which that liability is expressed. First, we constructed factor- 723

based polygenic scores (PGS) from genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of latent phenomic 724

factors derived in UK Biobank (UKB), together with internal and external disease-specific 725

diabetes (T2D) as the primary outcomes for comparative benchmarking because they 812

represented clinically important diseases across distinct domains and spanned settings in which 813

Social determinants of health (SDoH) were evaluated in the All of Us Research Program (AoU), 848

where structured social measures were available at sufficient depth for joint modeling with genetic 849

five domains: Economic Stability, Education Access and Quality, Healthcare Access and Quality, 851

Neighborhood and Built Environment, and Social and Community Context44. Candidate SDoH 852

variables  were initially reviewed across five All of Us surveys (The Basics, Lifestyle, Overall 853

Health, Healthcare Access & Utilization, and Social Determinants of Health; release v7; 854

(https://www.researchallofus.org/data-tools/survey-explorer/) by referencing the systematic 855

mapping developed by Hysong et al.45, which aligned All of Us survey items to HP2030 objectives. 856

The final analytic SDoH set was drawn from three of these surveys, as detailed in Table S6. 857

858

Primary European ancestry analyses used 29 SDoH variables chosen to provide broad coverage 859

across all five HP2030 domains. A temporally robust 16-variable subset was selected for 860

sensitivity analyses designed to reduce, though not eliminate, concern about reverse causation 861

in the prevalent-disease analyses. Those variables were selected on the basis of questionnaire 862

content and reference frame, prioritizing indicators intended to reflect relatively stable structural 863

or socioeconomic conditions and excluding items more likely to capture short-term states or 864

consequences of current illness. This classification was based on item wording and conceptual 865

stability rather than confirmed temporal ordering relative to disease onset. Because the primary 866

analyses use prevalent disease, even this restricted subset does not establish that measured 867

SDoH exposure preceded disease onset; instead, it serves as a sensitivity analysis designed to 868

reduce susceptibility to reverse causation. Cross-ancestry analyses used a harmonized 7- 869

variable subset from the AoU Basics survey with <1% missingness across populations. Variables 870

were recoded so higher values indicated greater social adversity. 871

For the 29-variable and 16-variable analyses, missing values were addressed using multiple 873

imputation by chained equations (M = 50 imputations). The 7-variable cross-ancestry analysis 874

was conducted using complete-case data because missingness was minimal. We first created 875
